verdict.rationale: Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol gives each agent interaction an RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signature (aligned with web-bot-auth). Signatures are tagged per interaction, protected against replay with timestamps and nonces, and verifiable by merchants against Visa's public JWKS. The public reference implementation includes an agent-registry and a cdn-proxy verifier, explicitly so merchants can distinguish credentialed agents from anonymous bots. Missing for 10: independent hands-on corroboration that merchant-side signature verification works in production, and no documented graded trust tiers beyond signature-based recognition.

support.subject: As a merchant, agents identify themselves verifiably — registered profiles, signatures, or trust tiers — so I can tell trusted agent traffic from anonymous bots

citations.quote: By presenting a secure digital signature with every interaction, a merchant can verify that an agent is legitimate and has the user's permission to act.
Cryptographically Verify Agent Intent: Instantly distinguish a legitimate, credentialed agent from an anonymous bot.
Agents include timestamps (created, expires) and nonces in the signature. Servers are able to reject reused or expired signatures, thereby preventing replay attacks.
These snippets demonstrate the use of public keys and how to construct the signature_base strings, which are the critical first steps in verifying an agent's signature on your end.
